claim: Adult human skin harbors potent oncogenic mutations without any functional or morphological consequences.
source: Adult human skin harbors potent oncogenic mutations without any functional or morphological consequences.
evidence: This is a general statement about adult human skin that is supported by the citation that follows it in the manuscript.

claim: Mutant clones that persist in the tissue are both limited and uniform in size, irrespective of a mutation's mitogenic potential.
source: A striking feature of this surprising tolerance is that mutant clones that persist in the tissue are both limited and uniform in size, irrespective of a mutation's mitogenic potential (Martincorena et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Martincorena et al., 2015.

claim: Gain-of-function mutant p53 clones grow extensively in naive epidermis.
source: In murine skin, gain-of-function mutant p53 clones grow extensively in naive epidermis, yet appear growth-inhibited when induced in a tissue premutagenized via acute exposure to UV.
evidence: This claim is supported by the citation to Murai et al., 2018 that follows in the text.

claim: Mutant p53 clones appear growth-inhibited when induced in a tissue premutagenized via acute exposure to UV.
source: In murine skin, gain-of-function mutant p53 clones grow extensively in naive epidermis, yet appear growth-inhibited when induced in a tissue premutagenized via acute exposure to UV.
evidence: This claim is supported by the citation to Murai et al., 2018 that follows in the text.

claim: UV radiation introduced mutations that were able to compete with expanding p53 clones, limiting their size.
source: This suggests that the UV radiation introduced mutations that were able to compete with expanding p53 clones, limiting their size (Murai et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Murai et al., 2018.

claim: Interclone growth inhibition may contribute to epithelial homeostasis in aged tissues.
source: This model of interclone growth inhibition may contribute to epithelial homeostasis in aged tissues, which contain a multitude of established mutations (Bowling et al., 2019; Higa and DeGregori, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bowling et al., 2019 and Higa and DeGregori, 2019.

claim: Aged tissues contain a multitude of established mutations.
source: This model of interclone growth inhibition may contribute to epithelial homeostasis in aged tissues, which contain a multitude of established mutations (Bowling et al., 2019; Higa and DeGregori, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bowling et al., 2019 and Higa and DeGregori, 2019.

claim: Activating mutation in β-catenin leads to ectopic hair follicle growths, which regress and are permanently eliminated.
source: Activating mutation in β-catenin leads to ectopic hair follicle growths, which regress and are permanently eliminated (Brown et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Brown et al., 2017.

claim: Pik3ca is the most commonly mutated oncogene in epithelial cancer.
source: Epidermal activation of Pik3ca, the most commonly mutated oncogene in epithelial cancer, induces clones which are more proliferative than wild type (WT).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Epidermal activation of Pik3ca induces clones which are more proliferative than wild type.
source: Epidermal activation of Pik3ca, the most commonly mutated oncogene in epithelial cancer, induces clones which are more proliferative than wild type (WT).
evidence: This claim is supported by the citation to Ying et al., 2018 that follows.

claim: Pik3ca-activated clones are lost as the oncogenic progenitors are removed from the tissue due to an inability to self-renew.
source: However, they too are lost as the oncogenic progenitors are removed from the tissue due to an inability to self-renew (Ying et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ying et al., 2018.

claim: Single-cell activation of oncogenic Hras (HrasG12V) results in formation of persistent clones within the interfollicular epidermis (IFE).
source: To answer this question, we use mouse skin and single-cell activation of oncogenic Hras (HrasG12V) which we previously demonstrated results in formation of persistent clones within the interfollicular epidermis (IFE) (Beronja et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Beronja et al., 2013.

claim: HrasG12V promotes an early and transient clonal expansion driven by increased progenitor renewal.
source: We observed that HrasG12V promotes an early and transient clonal expansion driven by increased progenitor renewal that is replaced with an increase in progenitor differentiation leading to reduced growth.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript, particularly in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Increased progenitor renewal in HrasG12V clones is replaced with an increase in progenitor differentiation leading to reduced growth.
source: We observed that HrasG12V promotes an early and transient clonal expansion driven by increased progenitor renewal that is replaced with an increase in progenitor differentiation leading to reduced growth.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript, particularly in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: HrasG12V clones contain two populations: renewing progenitors along the edge and differentiating ones within the central core.
source: We attribute this dynamic effect to emergence of two populations within oncogenic clones: renewing progenitors along the edge and differentiating ones within the central core.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3.

claim: Clone expansion is accompanied by progressive enlargement of the core and diminishment of the edge compartment.
source: As clone expansion is accompanied by progressive enlargement of the core and diminishment of the edge compartment, the intraclonal competition between the two populations results in stabilized oncogenic growth.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3.

claim: Intraclonal competition between edge and core populations results in stabilized oncogenic growth.
source: As clone expansion is accompanied by progressive enlargement of the core and diminishment of the edge compartment, the intraclonal competition between the two populations results in stabilized oncogenic growth.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Rassf5 is a novel regulator of progenitor fate choice.
source: To identify the molecular mechanism of HrasG12V-driven differentiation, we screened known Ras-effector in vivo and identified Rassf5 as a novel regulator of progenitor fate choice that is necessary and sufficient for oncogene-specific differentiation.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Rassf5 is necessary for oncogene-specific differentiation.
source: To identify the molecular mechanism of HrasG12V-driven differentiation, we screened known Ras-effector in vivo and identified Rassf5 as a novel regulator of progenitor fate choice that is necessary and sufficient for oncogene-specific differentiation.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 5.

claim: Rassf5 is sufficient for oncogene-specific differentiation.
source: To identify the molecular mechanism of HrasG12V-driven differentiation, we screened known Ras-effector in vivo and identified Rassf5 as a novel regulator of progenitor fate choice that is necessary and sufficient for oncogene-specific differentiation.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 5.

claim: Asymmetric divisions occurred in approximately 44% of cases in control head skin epidermis.
source: Analysis of control (R26mT/mG) head skin epidermis showed that asymmetric divisions, once considered the predominant division type of epidermal progenitors, occurred in approximately 44% of cases, and that symmetric renewal was nearly perfectly balanced by symmetric differentiation (29% vs. 27%) (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: In control epidermis, symmetric renewal was nearly perfectly balanced by symmetric differentiation (29% vs. 27%).
source: Analysis of control (R26mT/mG) head skin epidermis showed that asymmetric divisions, once considered the predominant division type of epidermal progenitors, occurred in approximately 44% of cases, and that symmetric renewal was nearly perfectly balanced by symmetric differentiation (29% vs. 27%) (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: HrasG12V expression results in a significant increase in symmetric renewal (48%).
source: In contrast, we observed a striking change in progenitor division type following expression of HrasG12V, with a significant increase in symmetric renewal (48%) and a significant decrease in symmetric differentiation (10%) (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: HrasG12V expression results in a significant decrease in symmetric differentiation (10%).
source: In contrast, we observed a striking change in progenitor division type following expression of HrasG12V, with a significant increase in symmetric renewal (48%) and a significant decrease in symmetric differentiation (10%) (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Epidermal progenitors in the control tissue had a renewal rate of ~0.5.
source: Epidermal progenitors in the control tissue had a renewal rate of ~0.5 (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: A renewal rate of ~0.5 is expected to maintain a stable population of basal progenitors long term and ensure neutral tissue growth.
source: Such a rate is expected to maintain a stable population of basal progenitors long term and ensure neutral tissue growth.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about tissue homeostasis.

claim: HrasG12V-expressing progenitors showed higher renewal rate of 0.69.
source: HrasG12V-expressing progenitors showed higher renewal rate of 0.69, which implies that oncogenic Hras, unlike single-cell expression of activated Pik3ca (Ying et al., 2018), promotes progenitor cell renewal.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Oncogenic Hras promotes progenitor cell renewal, unlike single-cell expression of activated Pik3ca.
source: HrasG12V-expressing progenitors showed higher renewal rate of 0.69, which implies that oncogenic Hras, unlike single-cell expression of activated Pik3ca (Ying et al., 2018), promotes progenitor cell renewal.
evidence: This claim is supported by data in the manuscript and citation to Ying et al., 2018.

claim: HrasG12V-expressing progenitors could support expansion and long-term maintenance of oncogenic clones.
source: It also suggests that in contrast to loss of cellular fitness we observed in oncogenic Pik3ca epidermis (Ying et al., 2018), HrasG12V-expressing progenitors could support expansion and long-term maintenance of oncogenic clones.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed renewal rate and comparison to Pik3ca.

claim: At 24 weeks, Hras clones were significantly larger than WT clones.
source: At this point, Hras clones were significantly larger that WT clones but were smaller than anticipated based on the high renewal rate (0.69) at clone initiation.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1G,H.

claim: At 24 weeks, Hras clones were smaller than anticipated based on the high renewal rate (0.69) at clone initiation.
source: At this point, Hras clones were significantly larger that WT clones but were smaller than anticipated based on the high renewal rate (0.69) at clone initiation.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1G,H and comparison to expected growth.

claim: Apoptosis was not significantly different between WT and oncogene expressing epidermis.
source: We first investigated apoptosis or senescence as a means to control clone growth but neither were significantly different between WT and oncogene expressing epidermis, (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Senescence was not significantly different between WT and oncogene expressing epidermis.
source: We first investigated apoptosis or senescence as a means to control clone growth but neither were significantly different between WT and oncogene expressing epidermis, (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Additional mechanisms of growth suppression are at play to curtail the expansion of HrasG12V progenitor cells.
source: This suggests that additional mechanisms of growth suppression are at play to curtail the expansion of HrasG12V progenitor cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that apoptosis and senescence do not explain the restricted growth.

claim: EdU+ labeling of single cells was restricted to the progenitors in the K10- basal layer at 30 min after EdU pulse.
source: We first gave animals a pulse of EdU and 30 min later processed the tissue for standard confocal imaging (Figure 2A). We observed EdU+ labeling of single cells throughout the tissue that was restricted to the progenitors in the K10- basal layer (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: At 2 hr after EdU pulse, there were sporadic EdU+/BrdU+ single cells and a population of EdU+/BrdU- cells, in which ~15% of cells have already divided but not differentiated.
source: We followed the EdU pulse with administration of BrdU 2 hr later (Figure 2A). This resulted in the appearance of sporadic EdU+/BrdU+ single cells and a population of EdU+/BrdU- cells, in which ~ 15% of cells have already divided but not differentiated (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: By 24 hr all EdU+/BrdU- cells were found as doublets and in both basal (K10-) and differentiated K10+ suprabasal layers.
source: By 24 hr all EdU+/BrdU- cells were found as doublets and in both basal (K10-) and differentiated K10+ suprabasal layers (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Cell fate choices scored by CFI assay are not significantly different from cell fate choices scored via intravital imaging.
source: We next compared the frequency of cell division types in control epidermis as measured by CFI with that obtained using intravital two-photon imaging of LV-CreER-transduced single cells (Figures 1E and 2D). We observed no significant differences between the two assays, suggesting that in CFI we have a valid and direct method for quantifying cell fate decision within the adult murine epidermis.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 1E and 2D.

claim: Oncogenic clones undergo more symmetric renewal initially, but by 8–10 weeks of growth the proportion of symmetric renewal divisions decreased and returned to rates observed in WT clones.
source: We observed that oncogenic clones undergo more symmetric renewal initially, but by 8–10 weeks of growth the proportion of symmetric renewal divisions decreased and returned to rates observed in WT clones (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Early increase in symmetric renewal was accompanied by reduction in the rates of symmetric differentiation and asymmetric divisions, which also returned to WT levels by 8–10 weeks.
source: Early increase in symmetric renewal was accompanied by reduction in the rates of symmetric differentiation and asymmetric divisions, which also returned to WT levels by 8–10 weeks (Figure 2G,H).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2G,H.

claim: WT progenitors maintained a renewal rate of ~0.5 throughout the duration of the study.
source: The WT progenitors maintained a renewal rate of ~0.5 throughout the duration of the study, consistent with a neutral growth potential of a homeostatic tissue (Figure 2I).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: HrasG12V-expressing progenitors showed an increase in renewal rate to ~0.70–0.85 in the initial 8 weeks, but then fell to ~0.55 over the next several weeks.
source: In contrast, the HrasG12V-expressing progenitors showed an increase in renewal rate to ~0.70–0.85 in the initial 8 weeks, but then fell to ~0.55 over the next several weeks as differentiating and asymmetric cell divisions increased (Figure 2I).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Oncogene expressing cells had a higher rate of EdU incorporation than WT, and the rates were largely stable over 24 weeks.
source: We also measured proliferation rates in control and HrasG12V clones over the same period, and observed that while oncogene expressing cells had a higher rate of EdU incorporation than WT, the rates were largely stable over 24 weeks (Figure 2J).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: Clonal expansion driven by a single oncogenic lesion is dependent on the cellular mechanisms of progenitor proliferation and renewal, with fluctuating rates of cell fate choice being the dominant determinant of growth dynamics.
source: Together, this suggests that clonal expansion driven by a single oncogenic lesion is dependent on the cellular mechanisms of progenitor proliferation and renewal, with fluctuating rates of cell fate choice being the dominant determinant of growth dynamics (Figure 2K).
evidence: This is an inference based on the data presented in Figure 2.

claim: Cell density increases between two and four weeks but then remains stable as highly renewing clones transition to more differentiating clones.
source: We observed that cell density increases between two and four weeks but then remains stable as highly renewing clones transition to more differentiating clones.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Cell density does not drive the switch in progenitor renewal.
source: This lack of temporal correlation suggested that cell density does not drive the switch in progenitor renewal.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of correlation between cell density and renewal rate changes.

claim: The shape of expanding HrasG12V clones appeared to be relatively round, irrespective of their age and size.
source: We noted that the shape of expanding HrasG12V clones appeared to be relatively round, irrespective of their age and size (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: HrasG12V clone circularity is maintained over time.
source: Indeed, this was confirmed through analysis of HrasG12V clone circularity (Figure 3D) and further implied that, as clones expand, their area increases at a greater rate than their circumference.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: As clones expand, their area increases at a greater rate than their circumference.
source: Indeed, this was confirmed through analysis of HrasG12V clone circularity (Figure 3D) and further implied that, as clones expand, their area increases at a greater rate than their circumference.
evidence: This is an inference based on the circularity data.

claim: Both edge and inner cell populations enlarged in absolute terms.
source: To test this, we quantified the number of edge and inner cells in HrasG12V clones and observed that while both populations enlarged in absolute terms (Figure 3E), the relative abundance of inner cells increased from 14 to 45% and edge cells decreased from 86 to 55% over time (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The relative abundance of inner cells increased from 14 to 45% and edge cells decreased from 86 to 55% over time.
source: To test this, we quantified the number of edge and inner cells in HrasG12V clones and observed that while both populations enlarged in absolute terms (Figure 3E), the relative abundance of inner cells increased from 14 to 45% and edge cells decreased from 86 to 55% over time (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Edge cells underwent significantly more symmetric renewing divisions than inner cells in 10-week-old HrasG12V clones.
source: Using CFI assay, we analyzed 10-week-old HrasG12V-clones and observed that although the rate of homeostatic asymmetric divisions was similar between edge and inner cells, they significantly differed in the ratio of growth regulating symmetric fate choices (Figure 3G). Although edge cells underwent significantly more symmetric renewing divisions, inner daughter cells more often chose differentiated cell fates.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Inner daughter cells more often chose differentiated cell fates than edge cells in 10-week-old HrasG12V clones.
source: Using CFI assay, we analyzed 10-week-old HrasG12V-clones and observed that although the rate of homeostatic asymmetric divisions was similar between edge and inner cells, they significantly differed in the ratio of growth regulating symmetric fate choices (Figure 3G). Although edge cells underwent significantly more symmetric renewing divisions, inner daughter cells more often chose differentiated cell fates.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Edge cell population maintains progenitor renewal rate consistent with growth expansion (0.69).
source: From observed division types, we extrapolated the renewal rate and established that edge cell population maintains progenitor renewal rate consistent with growth expansion (0.69) while inner population is below the 0.5 threshold required for stasis, and therefore in a state of progenitor loss (Figure 3H).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Inner population is below the 0.5 threshold required for stasis, and therefore in a state of progenitor loss.
source: From observed division types, we extrapolated the renewal rate and established that edge cell population maintains progenitor renewal rate consistent with growth expansion (0.69) while inner population is below the 0.5 threshold required for stasis, and therefore in a state of progenitor loss (Figure 3H).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: WT cells adjacent to late-stage HrasG12V clones had a lower frequency of symmetric renewing divisions compared to WT cells not adjacent to HrasG12V clones.
source: We also analyzed the behavior of WT cells adjacent to late-stage HrasG12V clones. We observed that these cells had a lower frequency of symmetric renewing divisions, as compared to WT cells not adjacent to HrasG12V clones (Figure 3I).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: WT cells adjacent to HrasG12V clones had a significantly lower renewal rate (0.41) compared to distant WT cells (0.50).
source: This change was reflected by a significantly lower renewal rate (0.41) compared to distant WT cells (0.50) (Figure 3J).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3J.

claim: Progenitor renewal rates were high (~0.75) and not significantly different between control and test clones at E18.5 following low titer LV-Cre transduction.
source: At E18.5, we confirmed that epidermis was transduced at clonal density (Figure 4A,B), and used EdU/BrdU differentiation assay to quantify renewal rate in YFP+ clones (Ying et al., 2018). We observed that progenitor renewal rates were high (~0.75), and not significantly different between control and test clones (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Large field expression of HrasG12V resulted in a significant reduction in progenitor renewal rate (0.76 vs. 0.57).
source: We quantified progenitor renewal under large field expression of HrasG12V and discovered a significant rate reduction (0.76 vs. 0.57; p value < 0.001; Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Uniform field activation of HrasG12V using K14-Cre resulted in a progenitor renewal rate of 0.56.
source: We also used K14-Cre transgenic mice to generate E18.5 epidermis with uniform field activation of HrasG12V (Figure 4A,B), and observed that the tissue's progenitor renewal rate (0.56) showed no difference between LV-Cre- and K14-Cre-induced fields (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: A field of progenitor cells that ubiquitously express HrasG12V more often gives rise to differentiated daughter cells.
source: Our data imply that a field of progenitor cells that ubiquitously express HrasG12V more often gives rise to differentiated daughter cells, and this correlates with the changes we see develop over time in adult HrasG12V clones.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data presented in Figure 4C.

claim: The screen in WT epidermis did not identify any Hras effector enrichment in basal or suprabasal cells.
source: Our screen in WT epidermis did not identify any Hras effector enrichment in basal or suprabasal cells (Figure 4E), suggesting that in normal development Hras signaling is not a significant regulator of progenitor cell fate choice.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: In normal development Hras signaling is not a significant regulator of progenitor cell fate choice.
source: Our screen in WT epidermis did not identify any Hras effector enrichment in basal or suprabasal cells (Figure 4E), suggesting that in normal development Hras signaling is not a significant regulator of progenitor cell fate choice.
evidence: This is an inference based on the screen results.

claim: The screen in HrasG12V-expressing epidermis identified shRNAs targeting Rassf5 and Pik3ca as significantly enriched in basal cells.
source: In contrast, the screen in HrasG12V-expressing epidermis identified shRNAs targeting Rassf5 and Pik3ca as significantly enriched in basal cells (Figure 4F), consistent with their putative role as negative regulators of HrasG12V-mediated progenitor renewal.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Rassf5 and Pik3ca are putative negative regulators of HrasG12V-mediated progenitor renewal.
source: In contrast, the screen in HrasG12V-expressing epidermis identified shRNAs targeting Rassf5 and Pik3ca as significantly enriched in basal cells (Figure 4F), consistent with their putative role as negative regulators of HrasG12V-mediated progenitor renewal.
evidence: This is an inference based on the screen results.

claim: The screen identified shRNAs targeting Rassf4, Rgl2, and Rgs14 as significantly enriched in suprabasal cells.
source: The screen also identified shRNAs targeting Rassf4, Rgl2, and Rgs14 as significantly enriched in suprabasal cells (Figure 4F, Supplementary file 1), suggesting that these genes may positively regulate renewal in HrasG12V epidermis.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4F and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Rassf4, Rgl2, and Rgs14 may positively regulate renewal in HrasG12V epidermis.
source: The screen also identified shRNAs targeting Rassf4, Rgl2, and Rgs14 as significantly enriched in suprabasal cells (Figure 4F, Supplementary file 1), suggesting that these genes may positively regulate renewal in HrasG12V epidermis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the screen results.

claim: Activated Pik3ca can drive progenitor differentiation in the epidermis.
source: We were encouraged by the observed enrichment of Pik3ca shRNAs in basal progenitors, as our lab has previously shown that activated Pik3ca can drive progenitor differentiation in the epidermis (Ying et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ying et al., 2018.

claim: Rassf5, also known as Nore1a, is a Ras effector containing a Ras Association (RA) domain which directly binds to activated Ras.
source: Rassf5, also known as Nore1a, is a Ras effector containing a Ras Association (RA) domain which directly binds to activated Ras (Vavvas et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Vavvas et al., 1998.

claim: Rassf5 lacks enzymatic activity.
source: Like other RA domain family (RASSF) members, Rassf5 lacks enzymatic activity and is often epigenetically silenced in cancer (Donninger et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Donninger et al., 2016.

claim: Rassf5 is often epigenetically silenced in cancer.
source: Like other RA domain family (RASSF) members, Rassf5 lacks enzymatic activity and is often epigenetically silenced in cancer (Donninger et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Donninger et al., 2016.

claim: Rassf5 is methylated in the majority of esophageal and head and neck squamous cell carcinomas.
source: Notably, Rassf5 is methylated in the majority of esophageal and head and neck squamous cell carcinomas (Guo et al., 2015; Steinmann et al., 2009) and has been shown to inhibit Ras growth via senescence (Donninger et al., 2015) and apoptosis (Elmetwali et al., 2016; Park et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Guo et al., 2015 and Steinmann et al., 2009.

claim: Rassf5 has been shown to inhibit Ras growth via senescence.
source: Notably, Rassf5 is methylated in the majority of esophageal and head and neck squamous cell carcinomas (Guo et al., 2015; Steinmann et al., 2009) and has been shown to inhibit Ras growth via senescence (Donninger et al., 2015) and apoptosis (Elmetwali et al., 2016; Park et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Donninger et al., 2015.

claim: Rassf5 has been shown to inhibit Ras growth via apoptosis.
source: Notably, Rassf5 is methylated in the majority of esophageal and head and neck squamous cell carcinomas (Guo et al., 2015; Steinmann et al., 2009) and has been shown to inhibit Ras growth via senescence (Donninger et al., 2015) and apoptosis (Elmetwali et al., 2016; Park et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Elmetwali et al., 2016 and Park et al., 2010.

claim: Both Rassf5 transcript and protein were elevated in HrasG12V epidermis at E18.5 relative to WT control.
source: To discern if Rassf5 also regulates progenitor cell fate choice and is critical to HrasG12V-mediated differentiation, we first quantified its expression in HrasG12V epidermis at E18.5 and discovered that both its transcript and protein were elevated relative to WT control, indicating that activated HrasG12V can promote Rassf5 expression (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: Activated HrasG12V can promote Rassf5 expression.
source: To discern if Rassf5 also regulates progenitor cell fate choice and is critical to HrasG12V-mediated differentiation, we first quantified its expression in HrasG12V epidermis at E18.5 and discovered that both its transcript and protein were elevated relative to WT control, indicating that activated HrasG12V can promote Rassf5 expression (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed increase in Rassf5 expression in HrasG12V epidermis.

claim: Three independent shRNAs depleted Rassf5 mRNA by ~70% in keratinocytes.
source: We next identified three independent shRNAs which depleted Rassf5 mRNA by ~70% in keratinocytes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), and generated lentiviral constructs for concomitant expression of Rassf5 shRNAs and Cre (LV-Cre-shRassf5; Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Rassf5 depletion in large HrasG12V-expressing fields leads to a significant increase in progenitor renewal rate.
source: Our data show that Rassf5 depletion in large HrasG12V-expressing fields leads to a significant increase in progenitor renewal rate, with three independent shRNAs demonstrating the same effect.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Rassf5 is necessary for HrasG12V-induced progenitor cell differentiation in embryonic tissues.
source: This signifies that Rassf5 is necessary for HrasG12V-induced progenitor cell differentiation in embryonic tissues.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed increase in renewal rate upon Rassf5 depletion.

claim: Rassf5 may have a more general ability to regulate progenitor cell renewal.
source: We also observe increased renewal in control epidermis with one out of three shRNAs we used, which suggests that Rassf5 may have a more general ability to regulate progenitor cell renewal (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed effect in control epidermis.

claim: Rassf5-expressing HrasG12V clones were composed of fewer basal and relatively more suprabasal cells.
source: Whole mount imaging further implied that Rassf5-expressing HrasG12V clones were composed of fewer basal and relatively more suprabasal cells (Figure 5G).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Rassf5 promotes significant reduction in basal cell numbers and significant increase in the suprabasal to basal surface area.
source: We analyzed clone composition and observed that Rassf5 promotes significant reduction in basal cell numbers and significant increase in the suprabasal to basal surface area (Figure 5H,I).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5H,I.

claim: Rassf5 is sufficient to promote progenitor cell differentiation in HrasG12V-expressing embryonic epidermis.
source: Together this suggests that Rassf5 is sufficient to promote progenitor cell differentiation in HrasG12V-expressing embryonic epidermis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed effects of Rassf5 overexpression.

claim: Depletion of Rassf5 in adult HrasG12V epidermis specifically suppressed progenitor differentiation of inner cells.
source: Focusing on the difference in renewal rate between the edge and inner clone compartments (Figure 3H), we observed that depletion of Rassf5 in adult HrasG12V epidermis specifically suppressed progenitor differentiation of inner cells (Figure 5J).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5J.

claim: The overall progenitor renewal rate was significantly elevated in HrasG12V/shRassf5 tissues.
source: As a result, the overall progenitor renewal rate was significantly elevated in HrasG12V/shRassf5 tissues (Figure 5K).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5K.

claim: Rates of apoptosis and senescence were not significantly affected in adult HrasG12V/shRassf5 epidermis.
source: We also measured rates of apoptosis and senescence in adult HrasG12V/shRassf5 epidermis and found neither to be significantly affected (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: Rassf5 is a negative regulator of progenitor renewal in the inner core of HrasG12V clones in the adult epidermis.
source: These observations suggest that Rassf5 is a negative regulator of progenitor renewal in the inner core of HrasG12V clones in the adult epidermis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed effects of Rassf5 depletion.

claim: Early clones expressing HrasG12V and Rassf5 had a significant reduction in their basal cell population compared to HrasG12V clones alone.
